data.title: Lifelong rapamycin administration ameliorates age-dependent cognitive deficits by reducing IL-1β and enhancing NMDA signaling
data.authors: Majumder S; Caccamo A; Medina DX; Benavides AD; Javors MA; Kraig E; Strong R; Richardson A; Oddo S

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: C57BL6/129svj mice (n=20 per group): encapsulated rapamycin in food (14 mg/kg food) from 2 to 18 months, from 15 to 18 months, or control diet; Morris water maze; brain cytokines, p-S6K, NR2B and CREB phosphorylation
data.finding: Mice were fed rapamycin in their food either from 2 months of age or only from 15 months, when age-related memory deficits were already present, and all were tested at 18 months in a water maze (20 mice per group). Mice treated from 2 months learned the hidden-platform location faster and spent more time in the target quadrant in the memory test (28.7 vs 21.3 seconds for controls), while mice started at 15 months did no better than controls. Both rapamycin groups had lower phosphorylation of S6K in the brain, a marker of mTOR activity. The improvement in the early-treated mice went together with lower IL-1beta in brain and hippocampus and higher phosphorylation of the NMDA receptor subunit NR2B and of CREB, which the authors propose as the route. Boundary: Mice of one mixed strain, normal ageing (not an Alzheimer model); the late-start arm showed no reversal of existing deficits, and the IL-1beta and NMDA links are correlations, not tested by blocking them.
data.abstract_excerpt: Understanding the factors that contribute to age-related cognitive decline is imperative, particularly as age is the major risk factor for several neurodegenerative disorders. Levels of several cytokines increase in the brain during aging, including IL-1β, whose levels positively correlate with cognitive deficits. Previous reports show that reducing the activity of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) extends lifespan in yeast, nematodes, Drosophila, and mice.

extracted_findings.intervention: Encapsulated rapamycin in diet (14 mg/kg food), from 2 or from 15 months of age to 18 months
extracted_findings.effect: Early lifelong rapamycin prevents age-dependent spatial learning/memory decline; late start (15 months) does not reverse it
